newsitem.title: INDIA: Israel denounced at Non-Aligned meeting.
newsitem.headline: Israel denounced at Non-Aligned meeting.

text.p: More than 100 developing nations opened a two-day meeting of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) on Monday with calls for the expansion of the United Nations Security Council and denunciations of Israel.

United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan joined Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda in calling for the greater representation of poor countries on the powerful U.N. body -- one of the themes of the NAM ministerial conference.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat accused Israel of declaring "war against the peace process" in the Middle East.
"The Israeli government is going through a war of aggression against our people," Arafat told the meeting of NAM foreign ministers in the Indian capital.
Arafat said Israel had used U.S. vetoes in the U.N. Security Council to prevent action against Israel's plan to build 6,500 homes for Jews on land captured in the 1967 Middle East war.
Ties between Palestinians and Israelis plunged into crisis after the Israeli government broke ground on the settlement.
"It is a declaration of war against the peace process," Arafat said.

Colombian Foreign Minister Maria Emma Mejia said that as chair of the two-day NAM meeting, she had sent a letter to Annan requesting a special session of the U.N. General Assembly to discuss the Middle East.
"It is with deep concern that we have been observing the increasing deterioration in the peace process in the Middle East," Mejia said.
"We cannot but demand the immediate cessation of construction of Israeli settlements in Jabal Abdul Ghneim in East Jerusalem."
Middle East peace talks were halted after Israel began work last month on the new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, sparking daily clashes between Palestinians and Israeli troops.
U.N. reform and the Middle East were among a handful of issues sure to dominate the two-day meeting in New Delhi which was given unusual prominence due to the attendance of the U.N. chief and Arafat.

Arafat's last-minute decision to attend provoked a mild diplomatic storm as, for reasons of protocol, his presence at the ministerial conference required the NAM meeting to temporarily adjourn and call a special session on the Mideast.

Zimbabwe's Foreign Minister I.S.G. Mudenge, speaking for the African member nations, echoed Arafat's criticism of the Israeli settlement in East Jerusalem. "The settlements will throw the peace process into the abyss," he said.

Annan threw his weight behind efforts to expand the U.N. Security Council, whose permanent members currently are the five declared nuclear powers -- Britain, China, France , Russia and the United States.

"The United Nations still reflects, in some ways -- for example, in the Security Council -- the geopolitical realities of the 1940s," he said, adding that he hoped expansion of the council would lead to greater representation of non-aligned and developing countries.

India's prime minister said the U.N. must be reformed to meet NAM's aspirations, and called for a redoubling of efforts to wipe out nuclear weapons. New Delhi is pressing for a permanent seat on the Security Council.
"The process of nuclear disarmament has to be accelerated," said Deve Gowda, who faces a vote of confidence on Friday.
The Non-Aligned Movement, formed in 1961 at the height of the Cold War, has 113 members, most of them developing nations.
